blocks.text: Quick verdict

FloppyData is the cheaper choice by a factor of eight at small volumes: $10 for 10 GB against $80 at Oxylabs pay-as-you-go, with the same flat rate at every volume. Oxylabs is the better choice for hard targets, enterprise pipelines and any work where failed requests or compliance questions are costly: its pool is far larger and independently benchmarked, targeting reaches ZIP and ASN, and its scraper APIs remove anti-bot work. Use FloppyData for experiments, Oxylabs for production at scale.

FloppyData and Oxylabs are as far apart as residential providers get. FloppyData is a young budget brand charging a flat $1/GB across residential, mobile and datacenter traffic. This comparison helps you decide which workloads can live on budget bandwidth and which need enterprise infrastructure.

blocks.text: FloppyData in 2026: what you get

FloppyData sells proxies the way prepaid phone plans sell minutes: one flat $1/GB balance that works across residential, mobile and datacenter pools. Static residential IPs start at $1.79 each in monthly bundles (20 for $49) with unlimited bandwidth. It is one of the cheapest ways into residential traffic, but it is a newer brand with less independent benchmarking than the established names.

Strengths: Flat $1/GB on any volume; One balance across residential, mobile and datacenter; Cheap static residential bundles with unlimited bandwidth; Free cloud anti-detect browser. Weak spots: Newer brand with limited independent testing; Pool-size claims disputed by some reviewers; Mixed customer-support reviews.
Oxylabs in 2026: what you get

Oxylabs sells enterprise-grade proxy infrastructure with a strong reputation among large scraping teams. Its residential network is one of the two largest on the market (175M+ advertised IPs, 195 locations), targeting reaches city, ZIP and ASN level, and its scraper APIs bundle rendering and parsing so you buy results rather than gigabytes. The weak spot for smaller buyers is entry cost: pay-as-you-go runs $8/GB and the cheapest monthly rate needs a $2,500 commitment.

Strengths: One of the two largest residential pools available; Published 99.95% residential success rate; Strong scraper APIs that bill per result; Formal ethical-sourcing documentation for procurement. Weak spots: Expensive at low volume ($8/GB PAYG); Best rates need large monthly commitments; Residential trial goes through sales rather than self-service.
Pricing: FloppyData vs Oxylabs

FloppyData charges a flat $1/GB for rotating traffic, and the same balance works for residential, mobile and datacenter IPs. Static residential proxies are sold in monthly bundles from $1.79 per IP (20 IPs for $49), and static datacenter IPs from $0.79 per IP.

Oxylabs charges $8/GB pay-as-you-go for residential traffic. Monthly plans start with Starter at $30 for 5 GB ($6/GB) and a Basic tier around $100 for 20 GB, and the rate falls to $2.50/GB on the $2,500/month Corporate plan. Mobile traffic starts at $7.50/GB.

Buying 10 GB, you would pay about $10 with FloppyData and $80 with Oxylabs: a 88% saving in FloppyData's favour. At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because Oxylabs does not publish an exact price for that volume; FloppyData comes to about $100. Both FloppyData and Oxylabs work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

FloppyData does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. FloppyData lists '65M+ claimed (disputed)' and Oxylabs lists '175M+'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, FloppyData lists 148 (residential) countries and Oxylabs lists 195. On targeting, FloppyData offers country and city, while Oxylabs offers country, state, city, ZIP and ASN.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, FloppyData offers rotating or sticky sessions, and Oxylabs offers rotating and sticky sessions on residential and mobile. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Oxylabs wins. The deciding factor for Oxylabs: its pool size and Web Scraper API suit large crawls. The limitation on the FloppyData side: cheap, but with limited independent benchmarking.
SERP and rank tracking: Oxylabs. Oxylabs has the edge here. Why: its scraper API returns parsed search results. How FloppyData compares: workable for light tasks.

Social media and multi-account management: FloppyData. FloppyData has the edge here. Why: cheap static residential IPs and a free anti-detect browser. How Oxylabs compares: it works, but the pricing is built for volume, not a handful of accounts.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Oxylabs wins. The deciding factor for Oxylabs: city and ZIP targeting plus parsed e-commerce endpoints. The limitation on the FloppyData side: city targeting at a flat rate.

Ad verification and geo-testing: Oxylabs wins. The deciding factor for Oxylabs: broad geo coverage with ASN targeting. The limitation on the FloppyData side: limited targeting depth and published data.
Tight budgets: FloppyData. FloppyData has the edge here. Why: a flat $1/GB on any volume. How Oxylabs compares: entry pricing is among the highest in this comparison.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. FloppyData: No free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations. Oxylabs: Residential trial arranged through sales, once per customer. Verification and payment rules differ too. FloppyData: Light. Oxylabs: Business verification on larger accounts. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test FloppyData and Oxylabs before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle FloppyData vs Oxylabs faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (FloppyData: no free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations; Oxylabs: residential trial arranged through sales, once per customer).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, FloppyData comes out ahead in 2, Oxylabs in 4, and 0 are ties. That makes Oxylabs the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: FloppyData is strongest for small budgets and experiments, while Oxylabs is strongest for large scraping pipelines with steady volume. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
